scenarios.name: R1: a match starts from a full 48-card deck and 12 cards are dealt in round 1, leaving 36
R1: four rounds from setup complete session 1 and the match moves on to session 2
R2: in round 5 an empty deck is refilled to 48 before the deal, leaving 36
R2: round 2 does not refill the deck (24 cards become 12)
R3: after the 4th round of a session the deck is empty
R4: with an all-Red deck every face-up card offered is Red
R5: round 3 pick order is seats 3, 4, 1, 2, so seat 2 picks last and only T4 is left
R6: a picker may gift to any opponent but never to itself
R7: kept, gifted and hidden Red cards count, so seat 1 with 1 Red before round 4 ends on 4 Red (one stack, 3 points) and the others discard 3 loose
R8: three gifts to seat 1 give it 5 Red (3+1); seat 2 discards 3 loose; seats 3 and 4 keep 2
R9: the hidden card counts for the picker, so seat 1 with no gifts still totals 2 Red
R10: the last picker in round 2 (seat 1) sees only T4 but still chooses which card to keep and whom to gift
R11: a mid-session round only advances the round, with no session score
R12: at the session end, public and hidden counts add up to totals before scoring
R13: a total of 7 gives 1 stack and 3 loose (seat 1 scores 3); a total of 6 gives 1 stack and 2 loose kept (seat 2 scores 5)
R14: players tied on the highest loose value all discard (Red 3,3,3,3; Blue loose 2,2,1,0)
R15: Red total 5 with a Red max loose of 2 scores 3+1 = 4
R16: the session score adds to game_total, and best_session_score changes only when beaten
R17: after the session-end reset the next session starts and round 5 adds no score
R18: the game ends after round 12; seat 1 wins on game_total plus tie-break
R19: seats tied on game_total and best_session_score share the win; a lower best loses the tie

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 4. The 4 triplets per round, 12 cards per colour and the rotating first pick are all sized to 4 seats. The game is about counting cards and gifting tactically against several rivals, and it needs 3 opponents to choose among as gift targets.
The source has no communication phase. Adding one would add a mechanic.

spec_choices.what: The whole pick (triplet, which card to keep, receiver) is asked as one choice from a generated list
spec_choices.why: The source resolves the pick as a single action. One question keeps it atomic and offers only legal combinations.
best_session_score is far below 1000, so game_total always dominates and the best session only breaks ties.

spec_choices.what: totals, stacks, loose and max_loose kept as 4-element lists in the order Red, Blue, Green, Yellow
spec_choices.why: The rules name these values, so they are declared, and lists keep the attribute count manageable.

A thoughtful player counts the unseen cards to estimate opponents' hidden colours, completes stacks of 4, and gifts cards that push a rival into a majority-loose discard or past a stack boundary that breaks their leftovers.

simplifications.what: Shuffling and dealing from the top is modelled as drawing 12 cards at random without replacement from the deck list each round, with the deck refilled only at rounds 1, 5 and 9
simplifications.why: This has the same distribution as one shuffle per session followed by top-card dealing, and it is the engine's way to draw.

simplifications.what: The session-end reveal is a broadcast of hidden counts rather than a change in visibility
simplifications.why: Attribute visibility is fixed. Announcing the values gives everyone the same information.

variation.original_summary: Gracias is a 3-6 player set-collection game over three sessions of four rounds. Each round players draft triplets of cards (two face-up, one face-down), keep one face-up card, hide the face-down card and must gift the other face-up card to an opponent. At each session end, cards in a colour are bundled into 5-stacks, the majority holder of each colour's face-up excess discards it, and players score surviving face-up cards plus stacks.

review.evidence: The forced gift and the majority discard mean no fixed rule wins. 'Always keep the first card and gift to the left' hands the left neighbour cards blindly and can push yourself into majorities. Seats rotate the start player. The previous variation kept this, so no simple policy dominates.

The previous variation dealt every card as an independent random draw, and scores turned on totals mod 3. The deal alone gave a session-score standard deviation of about 2 points, while skilled choices were worth about 1 to 2 points per session. Its testers estimated 60-70% of the result was chance, with a skilled player winning only 35-40% against a 25% baseline. The original's finite 108-card deck and draft give somewhat more control, but it is still noisy.

Choosing which card to keep, whom to burden and which majorities to risk gives a weak player a score. Card counting, reading rivals' hidden cards and timing gifts against the leader leave room to improve.

The original has hidden face-down cards and an inferable deck. The previous variation dropped the finite deck, so the 4 hidden cards per opponent per session were uniformly unknown. Targeted gifts became guesses and there was no card counting.
Stacks, discards and scores are pure arithmetic on card counts, and the winner is the highest total.

The previous variation needed 12 independent random draws per round against a limit of 1, and the engine has no multi-card random deal. The original's 6 colours, 108 cards and up to 6 players also inflate attributes.

problems: P1: Randomness exceeds the platform: dealing 12 independent cards per round is 12 random draws, the limit is 1, and there is no multi-card random operation.
P2: Luck swamps skill: independent per-card randomness plus mod-3 scoring makes the deal decide about 60-70% of results.
P3: No inference: with an infinite deck, opponents' hidden cards cannot be counted, so gifts aimed at rivals are guesses.
P4: The majority discard was nearly meaningless: with loose values of 0-2, a loose 2 was almost always discarded and the majority comparison only mattered for loose 1.
P5: The previous variation removed the draft (the original's triplet choice), the main decision that reduces deal variance.
P6: The stack value (2 points for 3 cards) made completing versus spoiling a rival's stack a small, hard-to-read swing.

changes.what: Use a finite 48-card deck (12 per colour), shuffled once at the start of each session (rounds 1, 5 and 9 only). Each round, deal by removing the top 12 cards of the shuffled list into 4 triplets.
changes.why: One shuffle per session is a single random draw, and dealing becomes list removal, the supported workaround. No round has more than one draw.

changes.what: All 48 cards are used every session. Face-up cards, keeps and gifts are public, so each colour's hidden total among opponents equals 12 minus all public cards of that colour minus your own hidden cards of it.
changes.why: Card counting lets players infer what rivals are hiding, so gifts that push a rival into a majority or away from a stack are planned rather than guessed.

changes.what: Restore the triplet draft. Each round, the 4 triplets are laid out with their two face-up cards shown. Players pick in turn, the start seat rotating each round. Each pick names the triplet, which face-up card to keep and which opponent receives the other.
changes.why: Players choose among offers instead of receiving a private random deal, so decisions outweigh the deal. Rotation gives each seat first pick 3 times and last pick 3 times. Picking in turn lets later players react to earlier gifts.
changes.fixes: P5: The previous variation removed the draft (also reduces P2)

changes.what: Use stacks of 4 worth 3 points each. Loose cards are worth 1 each, with loose = total mod 4 (0-3). Majority discard applies to the highest loose value per colour (ties all discard).
changes.why: Loose values now range 0-3 and genuinely differ between players. Completing a rival's stack (+3 to them) versus pushing them into the majority is a large, readable swing.
changes.fixes: P4: The majority discard was nearly meaningless; P6: The stack value made the swing small (also reduces P2)

changes.why: Four turn-based picks already use the full 4 choice steps per round. The conflict over who gets burdened is expressed directly through public gifts in turn order.
changes.fixes: P1: Randomness exceeds the platform (keeps the build within limits)

keeps: Three sessions of four rounds, with scores summed across sessions.
Triplets of two face-up cards and one face-down card, drafted in turn order with a rotating start player.
Keep one face-up card, hide the face-down card, and a forced gift of the other face-up card to an opponent.
Stacks protect cards, and the majority holder of loose cards in a colour discards them, ties included.
Highest total wins, with the best single session as tie-break.

recommendation.reason: A finite deck and the draft bring randomness within the limit and make hidden cards countable. Stacks of 4 with loose 0-3 make the gift decision meaningful.

variation.name: Gracias: The Counted Gift
variation.summary: Four players draft triplets from a finite 48-card deck. Each keeps one face-up card, hides the face-down card and must gift the other face-up card to a rival. Card counting reveals what rivals are hiding, and gifts are aimed to spoil their stacks or push them into the losing majority.
variation.rules:
SETUP
- 4 players in seats 1-4. 4 colours: Red, Blue, Green, Yellow.
- The deck has 48 cards: 12 of each colour.
- Each player has, for each colour, a public count and a hidden count, all starting at 0, plus a game total (0) and a best session score (0).
- The game has 3 sessions of 4 rounds each, 12 rounds in all.

EACH ROUND
1. Shuffle (rounds 1, 5 and 9 only). All 48 cards are shuffled into a random order. This is the only random event in the game. No other round shuffles.
2. Lay out. The next 12 cards are removed from the top of the deck and form 4 triplets, T1 to T4. Each triplet has face-up cards A and B and a face-down card H. The A and B cards of all four triplets are announced to everyone. The H cards stay secret.
3. Draft. Players pick one at a time. In round r, seat ((r-1) mod 4) + 1 picks first, then the others in increasing seat order, wrapping from 4 to 1. On their turn a player chooses one remaining triplet, which of its two face-up cards to keep, and which opponent receives the other face-up card. They may not gift to themselves and must gift. The choice is resolved and announced at once:
   - the kept card adds 1 to the picker's public count of its colour;
   - the gifted card adds 1 to the receiver's public count of its colour;
   - the H card is told only to the picker and adds 1 to the picker's hidden count of its colour;
   - the triplet is removed. The last picker takes the one remaining triplet but still chooses which card to keep and whom to gift.
4. Announce. All public counts of every player are announced.

SESSION END (after rounds 4, 8 and 12)
5. Reveal. All hidden counts are revealed. For each player and colour, total = public count + hidden count. Across the four players, each colour's totals sum to 12.
6. Stacks. For each player and colour: stacks = floor(total / 4), and loose = total - 4 × stacks, so loose is 0, 1, 2 or 3.
7. Majority discard. For each colour, find the highest loose value among the 4 players. If it is at least 1, every player whose loose equals it scores none of those loose cards (ties all discard).
8. Session score. Each player scores 3 points per stack plus 1 point per loose card not discarded, summed over the 4 colours. This is added to their game total. If it exceeds their best session score, it becomes their best session score.
9. Reset. All public and hidden counts return to 0. The next session begins with a fresh shuffle in its first round.

COUNTING NOTE (public information): during a session, the cards not yet seen by a player are their opponents' hidden cards plus the undealt deck, and the colour make-up of these is exactly 12 per colour minus every public card minus that player's own hidden cards.
variation.objective: After session 3, the player with the highest game total wins. If several players tie, the one among them with the highest best session score wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect: With the deck fixed and fully used each session, a player who tracks public cards can bound what each rival hides, especially in rounds 3-4 when only 16 hidden cards are unknown. A gift then becomes a calculated strike: giving a rival a third loose card in a colour where they likely lead the majority, or avoiding handing a fourth card that completes their 3-point stack. The draft with a rotating first pick lets players choose which risks to absorb, and seats are balanced. Simple policies lose: always taking the first triplet and gifting to the next seat feeds stacks and creates majorities blindly, and random play is exploited by counters. Hidden H cards still add chance, but the choice among offers, the 3-point stacks and the countable deck should shift results clearly toward skilled play. Talk is omitted: the 4 turn-based picks fill the choice budget, and the conflict over who gets burdened is expressed through public gifts.

balanced.evidence:
SEATS: the four seats are symmetric. Talk and choice are both simultaneous polls and every player gets the same deal structure, so there is no move-order or information edge.

PER-COLOUR SCORE (t = total cards of a colour, loose = t mod 3, stack = 2 pts). Loose can only be 0, 1 or 2, so loose 2 is always the highest value and is always discarded. Loose 1 scores only if some other player has loose 2 in that colour.
- t=0: 0
- t=1: 1 if an opponent has loose 2, else 0
- t=2: 0 (always discarded)
- t=3: 2
- t=4: 2 or 3
- t=5: 2
- t=6: 4

MARGINAL VALUE OF ONE MORE CARD: +0/1, then -1/0, then +2, and the pattern repeats. A gift can therefore help or hurt the receiver:
- receiver at loose 1: drops to loose 2 and loses up to 1 point;
- receiver at loose 2: completes a stack, +2;
- receiver at loose 0: +0 or +1.
The 'majority' label is literally computed correctly. It only bites on loose-1 holdings, but the computed rule is still consistent.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule, 4 players, about 12 cards each per session):
- 'Always keep A, gift left': no informed choice, so it gives up about 1 to 2 points per session versus a player who keeps the colour reaching 0 mod 3 and gifts cards that push opponents to loose 2. It loses whenever its deal is not better. It does not win or draw almost every time.
- 'Always keep B': symmetric to the above.
- 'Always gift to the same seat': feeds that seat when the gift completes stacks, so it can make that seat win. It is not self-protecting.

DOMINANCE: no option is strictly better whatever the opponents do, because the value of keeping and of each gift target depends on everyone's counts mod 3. No policy never loses. Every player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Steps 16 ≤ 20. Choice steps 2 (talk, choose) ≤ 4. Attributes 14 ≤ 20: per player, 8 colour counts, game total, best session, A, B, H and session score. Hidden elements 1 ≤ 3. Rounds 12 ≤ 40. The rules are complete: forced gift, no self-gift, 6 options, tie-break by best session then draw. The game is finite and scored by calc. Talk is simultaneous and fits a 4-player game where interests conflict (who gets dumped on, ganging up on the leader).

The problem is randomness. Each round deals 3 independent cards to each of 4 players: 12 independent random draws per round. Labelling them 'the single random event' does not reduce them to one draw. The limit is random_draws_per_round at most 1, and the engine has no single-operation multi-card random deal. Shared_deck_draw is only supported as remove/append on a list.

The repeated-game betrayal check is not applicable: there is no cooperate/defect pairing.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE: per session each player receives 4 hidden and 8 offered cards, all independently random. Final scores turn on each total mod 3, which jumps by 2 points per card (0 → 2 at the third card, 2 → 0 at the second). The rough standard deviation of a session score from the deal alone is about 2 points, about 3.5 over the game. Skilled keep/gift choices are worth about 1 to 2 points per session over a naive policy.

INFERENCE: weak. Each opponent has up to 4 hidden cards per session, each uniformly any colour. By rounds 3 and 4 an opponent's colour totals mod 3 are close to uniformly unknown, so targeted gifts (pushing a rival to loose 2) are largely guesses. With infinite independent cards there is no card counting. Talk is cheap and unbinding. Keep choices leak a little preference.

ALL PLAY WELL: decisions are symmetric and offset, so the winner is decided mainly by who was dealt colour counts landing on multiples of 3, i.e. by the deal. On top of this, three opponents' gifts add kingmaking noise.

ESTIMATE: about 60 to 70% of the result is chance. A skilled player wins perhaps 35 to 40% against a 25% baseline. That is not clearly favoured.

required_changes: Replace independent per-card randomness with a finite deck shuffled once per session, e.g. 48 cards, 12 per colour, as one random draw. Deal by removal from the list (the shared_deck_draw workaround). This gives at most 1 random draw per round.

Use the finite deck and public removals so players can count cards. Each player's hidden cards then become inferable from the remaining deck composition and from their keep choices, and gifts can be aimed with real inference.

Reduce deal variance and raise the decision share. Option 1: replace the private random H with a choice: each player picks one of two face-down cards they have seen, or deals come from a shared central offer picked in a snake order across rounds (as in the original's triplet draft).
Option 2: make the gift decision heavier, e.g. stack = 3 points so that completing a rival's stack versus pushing them to loose 2 is a large, readable swing.

Make the majority discard compare values that can actually differ, e.g. use loose = total mod 4 with stacks of 4, or compare raw face-up totals as in the original. As written, loose 2 is always discarded and the 'majority' only matters for loose 1.

balanced.evidence: PER-COLOUR SCORE TABLE (total = public + hidden; stacks = floor(t/4), loose = t mod 4). Format is score if your loose is not the highest / score if it is the highest (tied or alone). t0: 0/0. t1: 1/0. t2: 2/0. t3: 3/0. t4: 3 (immune). t5: 4/3. t6: 5/3. t7: 6/3. t8: 6 (immune). This gives three tensions. (a) The 4th card of a colour is worth +0 if your 3 loose were safe and +3 if they were the highest, so the value of a card depends on other players' counts. (b) A gift can hurt: it can push an opponent's loose from 2 to 3 so they alone are highest and score 0 instead of 2. A gift can also help: it can turn an opponent's 3 loose into a stack, moving them from 0 to 3. Gifting is therefore a real targeting decision. (c) Hidden H cards mean public counts understate totals. CARD FLOW: each round uses exactly 12 cards (4 triplets x 3), so 4 rounds use all 48 cards. Each player gets 8 cards of their own plus about 4 gifts, so about 3 per colour on average. Loose values cluster at 1-3, and the majority discard bites almost every colour. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule (highest total out of 4). (1) 'Always take the first remaining triplet, keep A, gift to the next seat': this ignores the table above. It will often keep a 3rd loose card into a colour where it is highest (scoring 0 instead of 2) and will gift 4th cards that complete opponents' stacks (+3 to them). It loses to sensible play and only beats random play by chance. It does not win or draw almost every time. (2) 'Always keep the colour you hold most of': this builds stacks, but it is exposed whenever it ends a colour on 3 loose (highest, 0). A sensible opponent gifts it a card to set up exactly that. It does not dominate. (3) 'Always gift to the current leader': reasonable as a heuristic, but blind gifting can complete the leader's stack. It is not dominant. No triplet, card or recipient choice is strictly better whatever others do, because every value is relative to the opponents' counts. In a 4-player highest-total game no policy guarantees never losing, and no cooperation premise is involved. SEAT ORDER: the first picker in round r is seat ((r-1) mod 4)+1. Pick positions by round within each session: seat 1 is 1st, 4th, 3rd, 2nd; seat 2 is 2nd, 1st, 4th, 3rd; seat 3 is 3rd, 2nd, 1st, 4th; seat 4 is 4th, 3rd, 2nd, 1st. This is a Latin square, so every seat holds every position exactly once per session. Each seat is also first picker 3 times in the 12 rounds. The pattern repeats each session, so seat 3 always makes the forced last pick and final gift of a session, and seat 4 always picks first in round 4. Being last has mixed value: no choice of triplet, but the final gift with the most information. I find no demonstrable net edge, so this is noted, not failed. All four players can realistically win. The tie-break (best session score, then a draw) is arithmetic.

playable.evidence: RULES COMPLETENESS. The deck size matches usage: 48 cards = 4 rounds x 12, with shuffles only in rounds 1, 5 and 9. Pick order, gift rules (must gift, not to self), the forced last triplet, reveal, stacks, loose, the ties-all-discard rule, scoring, reset and the tie-break are all specified with arithmetic. The game is finite at 12 rounds. Each pick is one sequential choice with at most 4 triplets x 2 cards x 3 recipients = 24 options, so 4 choice steps per round (limit 4). STEP TALLY. Per round: shuffle (when r mod 4 = 1) 1, layout 1, draft 4, announce 1, giving 7. Session-end steps carry `when r mod 4 = 0`: reveal/total 1, stacks/loose 1, max loose per colour 4 (player-to-player comparison needs the workaround of mirroring values into table attributes), discard+score 1, game total and best score 1, reset 1, giving 9. That totals about 16, within the limit of 20. The designer's figure of 15 is slightly low but the true count stays legal. Attributes: per player 4 public + 4 hidden + total + best = 10, plus table attributes (deck, triplets, 4 colour maxima). That is within 20 if counted per definition; it is tight, so loose values should be computed inline, not stored per player per colour. Hidden elements: H cards/hidden counts and deck order, 2 (limit 3). One random draw in a round (limit 1). No board, clock, judge, trading or binding agreement is needed. TALK: there is none, which is sensible. Choices are sequential with all public counts announced, so each player sees prior picks and gifts rather than guessing simultaneous moves. Talk would mostly add words, although an informal alliance against a leader is possible. Not a fixed-length cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: CHANCE SOURCES: the deck order sets which A/B cards appear in which round, and which H card lies under each triplet. Each player receives 4 random hidden cards per session, which affects whether colours reach 4. SKILL SOURCES: (1) Counting. The colour make-up of the unseen cards is exactly computable (12 per colour minus public cards minus own hidden cards), so opponents' likely hidden colours can be inferred, especially by round 4. (2) Reading opponents. Each pick reveals which colour a player kept and whom they targeted, which signals their hidden holdings and plans. (3) Planning against the threshold table. Aim for 4 (immune, 3 points) or 1-2 loose below the leader, and avoid ending on a lone highest 3. (4) Weaponised gifts that push rivals into the highest-loose discard. ALL-GOOD-PLAY CASE: the H draws create variance of a few points per session, but the outcome is shaped by draft order choices, gift targeting and how good players react to each other. The winner is not decided by the shuffle alone. Over 3 sessions (36 decisions per player), the random deal is a perturbation that good play can overcome. Estimated chance share is about 30-40%. A careful counter and modeller is clearly favoured over a thoughtless drafter, whose blind keeps and gifts cost several points per session (see the score table).

triage.reason: The game plays correctly. Each pick is offered as one combined option, such as 'T1: keep A (Yellow), give B (Red) to seat 2'. The rules do not prescribe option labels, and a single combined choice is a valid way to make the triplet, keep and gift decision. The tests fail only because they expect separate options named exactly 'T1', 'keep A' or 'Red', which the game never offers. The game's round and session progress (round 5, session 2 after 4 rounds) and the round-3 pick order (seats 3, 4, 1, 2) match the rules.
triage.guidance:
Do not assert that bare tokens like 'T1', 'T4', 'keep A' or 'Red' are offered as whole options. The game offers one combined option per pick, in the form 'Tn: keep A (Colour), give B (Colour) to seat k'. Either match against that actual option format, or test the rule through outcomes instead.
- R1: assert progress (round 5, session 2) and that session scores were produced. Do not assert specific offered labels.
- R2 and R4: with a given all-Red 12-card deck in round 2, check that every offered option's face-up colours are Red. Use the full option strings or a pattern on them. Alternatively, check that each player's public Red gains plus all their other public gains come only from Red, and that round and session advance to 3 and 1.
- R5: verify pick order by which seat acts in each turn of round 3 (3, 4, 1, 2). Do not require a particular seat to be offered 'T3' or 'T4'. Under the default 'first' choice, earlier pickers remove triplets, so a later seat only ever sees the remaining one.
- Any per-seat rule must use option strings that the game can actually present to that seat at that moment.
